title: I'm worried AI games are already starting to make traditional ones look inferior.
author: No_Departure7494
selftext:
No, they aren't mainstream yet - But when I hear that GTA 6 will have over 90 dynamic world events (Other estimates say 1,200) with 600,000 unique animations.... It's amazing that humans do that but imagine what machines will be able to produce in 10 years from now?

I am NOT talking about creativity. Efficiency. Seeing some of the stuff that's posted on here. Not one shots, but 1-3 month long projects. They're incredible. Sure they need fine tuning, proper story lines, etc - But in a month? 3 months? 

It's probably just me but if GTA 6 was released in 1-2 years from now and we compared it to what AI is making (Again, in terms of scale and efficiency), it would look far less impressive.

comments.author: OWazabi
comments.body:
Yes, from an objective point of view, it's over already.  
People will still do things because they can and enjoy doing it, but if you're talking strictly capabilities, in 10 years, then yes it's totally over.

There's many layers to it, and games are going to change radically many times.  
For example, 3D animation  
3D and custom animations are just the product of the fact we cannot generate video on demand as we want it.  
If we could, then there wouldn't be any need for those.  
Eventually, live video generation and world models replace these things entirely, and game engines aren't about 3D anymore, but more about a set of rules for the machine to evolve in, making the games a billion times more interactive and unique  
3D would be relevant to.... 3D printing probably c:

replies.author: xcdesz
replies.body:
Nothing is "over", except the old way of doing things.  Games will be easier to make, but making it easier will only make folks build bigger and better games, and continue to push the limits of the technology.  The only thing that ends is the old ways of doing things, and the old tools.  There will still be AAA games, but they will make GTA 6 look like Pong.

Its happened many times before in software development.  Compilers, IDE's, frameworks, game engines, all those things to make games more efficient to make... didn't wind up "ending" the industry.   Its only made the business expand, not collapse.

comments.author: RandomCSThrowaway01
comments.body:
>It's probably just me

It is. 

Forget "mainstream" - show me **one** "AI game" that competes with AA. Not AAA, I am not asking for that kind of scale. AA. You have a choice - Ori, Subnautica, Ghostrunner, No Man Sky, Hellblade: Semi's Sacrifice, Lies of P, Clair Obscur or Hades. 

You are saying AI games are already starting to make current ones feel inferior so I am asking for specific ones that made you feel that way. 

I am not arguing about 10 years from now, that's an eternity and even guessing what will happen by then is hard. I mean, there is a "utopia model" with extremely cheap and powerful intelligence for all. But we **also** have non-zero chances that all really good models will be locked away for government use only and the stuff available to the public will be much, much worse. OpenAI and Anthropic at least are trying to make that model reality lately with how incompetent they are at security, they have literally no idea what their agents are doing.

replies.author: RandomCSThrowaway01
replies.body:
>But the proof of concept? Absolutely.

So here's a thing - I **do not** disagree but LLMs performance drops as the project grows. It can one shot a whole landscape (as long as you don't look at the details) but then it needs 1.5-3h to model a single character or a detailed prop. It can build a prototype of a game in 30 minutes but then it takes an hour for a small feature that ties into other dependencies. 

This makes comparing prototypes and MVPs to finished games somewhat disingenuous. Like, prototyping is genuinely x30 speedup right now and it likely will be even faster. But if you are deeper into development then I genuinely feel it's closer to x2. Since a lot of the tasks ahead are really bottlenecked by LLM-unfriendly ecosystem like "let's make it fun for our target audience". I mean you can sure make a game fun for an LLM to play but that's probably not who can pay for it.

So I would refrain my judgement until we actually see such games released and how much of a gap it really makes. At the very least from my experience so far - even if we reduced time to code a feature or build an asset to zero you still need to explain what exactly you want which takes multiple iterations. And that's probably not going to change since not even you know what exactly you want - just that before you figured out various edge cases while coding/building it by hand and now you get to see the results first and fine tune them as you go with prompting. LLMs are usually not finding an "optimal" solution, especially since in a game "optimal" doesn't even exist, it's all subjective.

Mind you, again, I am not saying it won't be faster and larger. I merely don't buy the idea we will see, say, another GTA 6 level game in a year made by a smaller team (cuz that's what would make it "far less impressive"). Time will tell, maybe I will be wrong. That's just my personal take so far.

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
Lots of these threads, especially lately, but what always gets ignored is the cost of AI is basically fake right now. Anthropic and OpenAI are in the gutter and we’re living in a golden age of AI pricing. If and when they go public kiss these well priced plans goodbye. 

And on that note, how are we supposed to power all of this? It’s already straining the aged power grid now. People don’t want data centers in their backyard. And now everyone’s going to be what, creating their own AAA-level game assets and cutscenes around the clock?

I just don’t see it happening without some major changes in how we run these things.

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body: Okay, now this is an extremely intriguing response that could ultimately be the biggest deal breaker for the future of AI. Is this true? That the pricing is only going to get worse?

replies.author: geddy
replies.body:
Think about it- the two biggest players are hemorrhaging money on compute and hardware, while paying their bills (in the hundreds of billions) with investor money. This is the equivalent of paying off credit cards with more credit cards. Going public means they’ll have an influx of cash, but a need to please shareholders, so the current pricing model won’t work.

Look at what happened to Uber. They came in, offered ridiculously cheap rides, disrupted everything, and now prices are up since the early days around 90%. 

Businesses used to have a good idea, start a company, experience growth, but run into cash bottlenecks, then put out an IPO and go public to get retail investors (ie. Buckets of cash) and build their company. $1000 in Amazon when they went public (in 1997!) is worth millions now because those funds helped the company grow. Now the modern way to make money is get private investors on the hook, get everybody used to the service so that they can’t live without it, then go public to pay off the massive debt, then the early investors can cash out while retail investors hold the bag, and users get screwed with the high prices.

Whenever they decide to go public, the IPO is going to be a huge number because it has to be. They’re valued at some silly amount of money. But all that money is going to do is pay back the investors, then they will raise the price significantly, and everybody will be pissed except the billionaires who funded them in the first place. 

Anyway, this went a little bit off-topic. But the optimism behind this being so world changing stops for me
 as soon as you think about how are we going to power it, and how much are we going to pay for it?

comments.author: deReaLizedGames
comments.body:
I participated in a small local video game showcase last week, and not gonna lie the other peoples' games looked pretty damn rough compared to mine. There was another solo dev whose assets and animations would have looked so much better if they had used AI rather than trying to do it themselves by hand. Especially as a solo dev, 90% of people aren't going to be very good at every part of game development. Someone can be good at code but trash at 3d modeling. Or good at 3d modeling but not good at animation. Proper AI use can fill in the gaps even for someone who isn't entirely using AI in their production.

I don't think we've hit easy AA standards yet but I would argue that proper use of AI can lead to a significantly better game than what an amateur solo dev is capable of at this point.
